participation.text: Political transfer and border decisions affected people who did not control the timetable.

evidence.text: Military letters and later testimony preserve particular viewpoints, not a universal civilian account.

name: 1947: independence and the disruption of home
place: British India, especially Punjab and Bengal
geographicPrecision: Punjab-region anchor. No present-day sovereignty or detailed partition boundary is drawn.

interval.label: Independence and partition, August 1947
interval.note: Selected transition; neither national identity nor displacement began and ended in one month.

question: How can political independence and personal insecurity happen together?
summary: Independence ended British rule and opened new political futures in 1947. Partition also divided Punjab and Bengal, separated neighbors and placed families in danger. Official plans, an annotated boundary map, a September telegram and later testimony tell different parts of the story. Read them together to understand how a change of sovereignty could coincide with uncertainty about home, safety and belonging.

sections.title: Several decisions, not one instant
sections.text: Demands for independence and disagreements about political representation preceded the final division. The National Archives describes an accelerated transfer announced on 3 June 1947 to two governments, India and Pakistan. Independence ceremonies on 14 and 15 August came before the boundary announcement on 17 August. These dates mark different actions. A legal or ceremonial beginning did not ensure that a family knew which side its home would fall on, could travel safely, or could rely on familiar public services.

sections.title: Why Punjab and Bengal need separate attention
sections.text: Partition divided two very different regional settings, far apart on the subcontinent. The linked archival map of Punjab marks the awarded boundary and a Sikh demand with different line styles. It records a political disagreement, not simply a neutral line on empty land. Lahore, Amritsar and other places carried religious, commercial and personal attachments that a boundary could cut across. Bengal should not be treated as a smaller copy of Punjab. Its different local histories and later movements require their own evidence, which the locator map and oral-history examples begin to introduce.

sections.title: What an official report can reveal
sections.text: On 23 September the UK High Commissioner sent a telegram describing attacks on refugee convoys and columns in Punjab, including groups moving in opposite directions. Its numbered paragraphs organize places, incidents and reported casualties for officials. This format provides time-specific information, but it also reduces people to administrative categories. The report’s title, “Communal disturbances,” deserves examination: does that language explain who organized violence, who failed to protect people, or why a particular group was vulnerable? A document can be useful and incomplete at the same time.

sections.title: The work of rebuilding a life
sections.text: The National Archives’ oral testimony from Iqbal Singh’s aunt connects displacement to schooling, money, language and the meaning of home. She recalls having to learn Hindi, the different schools affordable for girls and boys, and her father’s persistent longing for the home left behind. When her family occupied a house left by Mr Ansari, she also imagined his loss. These memories make visible consequences that a boundary map cannot show. They are a later personal account, shaped by recollection, rather than a statistical description of all refugees.

citations.locator: Source 6: Learning Hindi; My father and Mr Ansari transcripts

sections.title: Neighbors cannot be reduced to categories
sections.text: The Partition Museum’s written summaries include Sunil Chandra Ghosh remembering help from Hamid Miyan and Hamida remembering shelter provided by a Hindu washerman. These accounts add acts of assistance across religious difference to a history of violence and displacement. They do not cancel the violence or establish how common such help was. They do prevent us from assuming that a religious category determines every individual’s actions. The atlas uses the museum’s published summaries; it does not claim to have verified full interview transcripts.

returnPrompt: What question would a family’s story add to a political map of independence?

familyActivity.title: A border and a home
steps: Use the linked map or the description on its reference card. The solid line marks the awarded border. The dashed line marks a demand. Which one tells you where the new boundary ran?
Choose a familiar place: a school, a family home or a market. Discuss what a political map would and would not tell someone about it.
Read the short account of mutual help below. Ask what this adds to an official report. Skip descriptions of violence if they are unsuitable for the reader.
familyActivity.explanation: The activity concerns evidence and belonging. It does not ask a child to role-play forced migration or assume what a survivor felt.

deeperReading.title: Read the map as an argument
deeperReading.text: The solid and dashed boundaries in CO 1054/76 have different meanings. One records the boundary as fixed in August 1947; the other records a demand running toward the Chenab. A reader who ignores the key could mistake both for official borders at different dates. The map’s Punjab focus is also a limit: it cannot explain the whole subcontinent. Pair it with Santokh Singh’s June 1946 letter about Sikh concerns and ask which attachments a population-based territorial settlement could fail to accommodate. The letter is an appeal to a powerful recipient, not an impartial survey of everyone’s position.

deeperReading.title: Authority, responsibility and hindsight
deeperReading.text: Lord Ismay’s personal note admits that danger was anticipated while describing the eventual scale as beyond what authorities expected. Read that statement in light of his position close to Mountbatten. He is explaining a crisis in which he had responsibilities, so his account deserves comparison with other evidence. The National Army Museum adds soldiers’ concerns about family safety and the division of military units. Together, these sources show that the institutions supposed to maintain order were themselves undergoing disruption. They do not make violence inevitable or remove responsibility from actors who organized or permitted it.

citations.locator: Law and order; Indian Army divided

deeperReading.title: After August: different clocks
deeperReading.text: The museum’s summary of Ila Banerjee places her family’s departure from East Bengal in 1950. Ijaz Khan’s account describes his father’s later return to Jalandhar and the welcome from former neighbors. These examples complicate any timeline that ends all movement and relationships in August 1947. The selected wider frame runs through 1950 to make an aftermath visible, not to close it. Rebuilding employment, education, possessions and social ties could take far longer; each requires local sources rather than an invented uniform timetable.

evidenceReading.title: Read an official document beside a personal account
evidenceReading.introduction: The two short quotations below come from the National Archives’ published transcripts. The remaining reading is a clearly labelled paraphrase.

items.label: Telegram heading · 23 September 1947
items.interpretation: This administrative heading groups events by a category. The numbered entries then report attacks on non-Muslim and Muslim refugees. Ask what the heading emphasizes and what explanation it leaves out.

citations.locator: Source 1: DO 142/416, telegram heading and Punjab paragraphs

items.label: Remembering home · later oral testimony
items.text: “Mr. Ansari must be missing his home, which became our home.”
items.interpretation: The speaker recognizes that the house her family gained was also a home another family lost. Her memory makes an ethical and personal connection across the border.

items.label: A later migration · museum summary, paraphrased
items.text: Ila Banerjee’s family left in 1950, after initially remaining in East Bengal.
items.interpretation: One chronology can challenge an overly tidy endpoint. It cannot establish the timing or reasons for every family’s departure.

placeStudy.title: Partition: two regions, different histories
placeStudy.description: A geographic locator for the Punjab and Bengal evidence. Boxes identify reading areas only. Use the linked archival Punjab map to examine its actual boundary claim; no current political borders or individual migration routes are drawn here.

points.label: Lahore · Punjab
points.text: A major place of attachment in the Punjab investigation. The archival map places Lahore west of the awarded boundary.

points.label: Amritsar · Punjab
points.text: Near Lahore geographically, but on the other side of the 1947 award. At this scale the markers are close together; the labelled list offers the same selection.

points.label: Delhi
points.text: The September telegram was sent from New Delhi. Its reports describe places beyond the office that sent it.

points.label: Barrackpore · Bengal
points.text: The museum summary places visits to Sunil Chandra Ghosh’s father here after the family’s move from East Pakistan. This is a place in one remembered relationship, not an endpoint for all refugees.

points.label: Mymensingh · East Bengal
points.text: The place associated with Ila Banerjee’s family before their departure in 1950, according to the museum summary. Later movement matters to the chronology.
